title: Why Kriti Sanon Swears By Daily Fibre and Electrolytes Over Just Protein
excerpt: The Bollywood star and wellness investor says most people overlook fibre — but nutritionists warn her approach needs context.
body:
• Kriti Sanon told Vogue India she takes fibre mixed with electrolytes daily, saying most people focus too heavily on protein alone
  • Clinical nutritionists say the combination supports digestion and hydration but offers no special synergy
  • Whole foods like oats, bananas, curd, and lentils can provide both nutrients naturally without supplements
  • People with kidney, heart, or blood-pressure conditions should consult a doctor before adding regular electrolyte drinks

In a fitness culture obsessed with protein shakes and macros, Bollywood actor Kriti Sanon is making a case for two overlooked nutrients: fibre and electrolytes. Speaking to Vogue India, the Cocktail 2 star revealed that her daily supplement routine centres on a fibre-electrolyte mix rather than the protein supplements that dominate gym culture.

"Everyone just talks about protein, protein, protein. And we forget to have fibre."

— Kriti Sanon, in an interview with Vogue India

Sanon said she mixes fibre with electrolytes in water and drinks it every day. It is worth noting that Sanon is also an investor and brand ambassador for Supply6, a Bengaluru-based D2C nutrition startup whose product line includes zero-sugar electrolytes and fibre supplements — adding a commercial dimension to her wellness advocacy.

What Nutritionists Actually Think

Edwina Raj, Head of Clinical Nutrition and Dietetics at Aster CMI Hospital in Bangalore, says combining fibre with electrolytes has practical merit — but it is not a magic formula.

"Fibre supports digestion, bowel regularity, gut health and fullness, while electrolytes such as sodium and potassium help maintain fluid balance, nerve function and normal muscle function," Raj told the Indian Express. The combination can be particularly useful for people who sweat heavily or exercise intensely.

But Raj is clear that there is no ideal ratio between the two, and the benefits depend entirely on a person's overall diet, activity level, and health status. No standard medical guideline prescribes a specific fibre-to-electrolyte formula for daily wellness.

Whole Foods vs. Supplements

For most healthy adults, Raj says supplements are unnecessary. "Fibre should primarily come from whole foods such as vegetables, fruits, oats, whole grains, beans, lentils, chickpeas, nuts and seeds," she explains. Electrolytes, too, are available naturally through coconut water, bananas, oranges, potatoes, curd, and ordinary water.

She recommends simple food pairings that deliver both nutrients: oats with banana and curd, chia seeds with fruit and yoghurt, or dal and vegetables with a potassium-rich side like potato or tomato.

For those who do opt for supplements, Raj offers a practical caution: increase fibre intake gradually. "Suddenly consuming large amounts of fibre may cause gas, bloating or constipation," she says. Adequate fluid intake alongside fibre supplements is essential to avoid digestive discomfort.

The Electrolyte Caution

Raj's sharpest warning targets electrolyte drinks specifically. Many commercial products contain significant amounts of sodium or added sugar, and daily consumption without a genuine need — such as heavy exercise or illness-related dehydration — can do more harm than good.

The World Health Organization recommends limiting sodium intake to less than 2,000 mg per day for adults. Adding an electrolyte drink on top of a normal diet could push someone over that threshold, particularly if the rest of their diet already includes processed foods.

Raj also draws a clear line between daily wellness drinks and oral rehydration solutions. "WHO's ORS formulation is designed specifically to replace water and electrolyte losses during diarrhoea and contains carefully measured amounts of sodium, potassium, citrate and glucose," she explains. An otherwise healthy person who exercises moderately does not need to replicate that formula daily.

The Bottom Line

Anyone with kidney disease, heart conditions, or blood-pressure problems should discuss regular electrolyte supplementation with a doctor rather than following a celebrity's routine, Raj advises. For healthy individuals, the message is simpler: eat your vegetables, drink enough water, and save the supplements for situations that actually demand them.

Sanon's instinct about fibre is directionally sound — most Indians do not consume the 25 to 30 grams of daily fibre that nutritionists recommend. But the delivery system matters less than the habit. A bowl of dal and sabzi may do the job just as well as a branded powder mixed into water.
